lines.text: Level: B2 · Topic: The Radio Station
lines.name: Level: B2 · Topic: The Radio Station

lines.text:
Behind the On-Air Sign — How Radio Still Reaches Millions

In an age of streaming and podcasts, traditional radio might seem like a relic. Yet it remains one of the most widely consumed media on Earth. A radio station is a factory of sound — and the machinery behind that sound is more complex than most listeners imagine.

The heart of the station is the control room. A mixing console — a wide panel of sliders, knobs, and meters — sits at the centre. The sound engineer adjusts levels in real time, balancing the radio host's voice against a music block or a jingle. An equalizer shapes tone. A compressor prevents sudden volume spikes. A pop filter — a mesh disc in front of the microphone — eliminates the burst of air from 'p' and 'b' sounds. Headphones allow the host to hear the broadcast as the listener hears it. A monitor speaker fills the room when headphones are removed.

The broadcast chain begins at the microphone and ends at the listener's radio receiver — a car radio, a portable radio, or a smartphone app. The signal travels from the microphone through an audio interface and a sound card into the computer, where audio software processes and records it. A digital recorder captures interviews. An XLR cable — the professional standard — connects microphone to console. A phantom power supply provides voltage to condenser microphones. A headphone amplifier drives multiple sets of headphones from a single source.

The studio itself is engineered for silence. Acoustic panels line the walls of the sound booth to absorb reflections. A soundproof booth — a room within a room — isolates the recording booth from corridor noise, air conditioning, and traffic. The on-air sign — usually a red light above the door — warns staff not to enter during a live broadcast.

Content is structured by format. A playlist sequences music. A jingle identifies the station between segments. A sound effect punctuates transitions. A station ID plays at the top of each hour. A commercial break funds the operation. A news bulletin delivers headlines. A weather update and a traffic report serve commuters. An interview segment brings guests into the studio. The producer coordinates all of this from behind the glass, communicating with the host via a cue card or a talkback microphone.

The team is specialised. The radio host presents. The producer plans. The sound engineer mixes. A news anchor reads bulletins. A traffic reporter monitors road conditions. A weather presenter interprets forecasts. A sales manager sells commercial time. The program director sets the station's overall tone and schedule. An intern learns every role.

The transmitter converts the audio signal into radio waves. An antenna on the roof or a tower broadcasts across the city. A frequency — measured in megahertz for FM or kilohertz for AM — identifies the station on a frequency dial. A volume knob and a tuner are the listener's only controls. Streaming has added a parallel channel: the same broadcast, delivered via the internet, accessible anywhere.

What makes radio endure is its intimacy. A single voice enters the listener's car, kitchen, or headphones — no screen required, no attention demanded beyond listening. That directness, that companionship, is something no algorithm has replicated.

lines.text: 'News' is an uncountable noun — always singular: 'The news is...', 'The news was...' Never 'the news were' or 'a news.' Use 'a piece of news', 'a news item', or 'a news bulletin' for countable reference. Other uncountable nouns often mistaken for plurals: 'information', 'advice', 'equipment', 'furniture.'

lines.text: ❌ "She suggested him to listen to the morning interview segment."
lines.name: ❌ "She suggested him to listen to the morning interview segment."

lines.text: ✅ "She suggested that he listen to the morning interview segment." / "She suggested listening to the morning interview segment."
lines.name: ✅ "She suggested that he listen to the morning interview segment." / "She suggested listening to the morning interview segment."

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggest him to listen). Correct patterns: suggest + that-clause (with subjunctive or 'should'): 'She suggested that he listen.' Suggest + gerund: 'She suggested listening.' Other verbs with the same restriction: 'recommend', 'propose.' Compare verbs that DO take object + infinitive: 'advise him to listen', 'encourage him to listen.'

lines.text: 'Say' + that-clause (no person): 'She said that...' 'Tell' + person + that-clause: 'She told the host that...' Never 'told that' without a person. Mnemonic: you always tell SOMEONE, but you say SOMETHING. 'Say' can take 'to': 'She said to the host that...' but 'tell' cannot take 'that' alone.

lines.text: ❌ "I used to listening to this station every morning when I was a student."
lines.name: ❌ "I used to listening to this station every morning when I was a student."

lines.text: ✅ "I used to listen to this station every morning when I was a student."
lines.name: ✅ "I used to listen to this station every morning when I was a student."

lines.text: 'Used to' + bare infinitive (past habit): 'I used to listen.' 'Be used to' + gerund (accustomed): 'I am used to listening.' 'Get used to' + gerund (becoming accustomed): 'I got used to listening.' The confusion arises because all three structures exist but with different meanings. Past habit = 'used to + infinitive.' Current habit = 'be used to + -ing.'

lines.text: 'Equipment' is uncountable — always singular: 'the equipment is', 'it needs.' Never 'equipments' or 'equipment are.' For countable reference: 'a piece of equipment', 'several items of equipment.' Similarly uncountable: 'machinery', 'apparatus', 'gear' (in this sense).

lines.text: 'Podcast' = pre-recorded audio available on demand. 'Radio' = traditionally live broadcast on a schedule. Many radio shows are now also released as podcasts. 'Streaming' = listening live via the internet. 'On demand' = listening whenever you choose.

lines.text: 'DJ' (disc jockey) = plays music, usually on a music station. 'Presenter' (BrE) = the person who presents any radio or TV programme. 'Host' (AmE) = same as presenter. 'Anchor' = the main presenter of a news programme.

lines.text: Listening to English-language radio is excellent for improving listening skills. BBC Learning English, BBC Radio 4, and NPR (American) are popular choices. Many stations offer 'listen again' features online. Podcasts with transcripts are especially useful for learners.
